title: FHSA Basics
subtitle: A deduction going in, like an RRSP. Tax-free withdrawals coming out, like a TFSA. Most registered accounts only offer one.

blocks.text: For a long time, Canadians saving for a first home had two options, and neither fit the job.
An RRSP gave a deduction, but taking money out for anything but retirement usually meant tax, with one narrow exception. A TFSA gave tax-free withdrawals, but no deduction going in.

In 2023, a new account arrived that took the best part of each. The First Home Savings Account, or FHSA, gives you a deduction going in, like an RRSP, and tax-free withdrawals coming out, like a TFSA. If you’re saving for a first home, it’s worth knowing well.
Get a tax break on your down payment, and keep every dollar of it.
blocks.detail: An FHSA cuts your tax now and lets you take the money out tax-free for your first home.
blocks.extra: Section 04 explains why opening one early matters most.

blocks.text: Two conditions, both fairly simple.

items.title: You live in Canada and you’re 18 or older. That’s the usual starting point for a registered account.
You’re a first-time home buyer. That means you haven’t lived in a home that you owned, or your spouse or partner owned, at any time this year or in the four years before.

blocks.text: That second condition trips people up. It doesn’t mean you have never owned a home. It means you haven’t lived in one you owned recently. Someone who sold a home eight years ago and has rented since can still qualify.

items.title: “Once you’ve owned a home, you can never open an FHSA again.”
items.text: Not true. The rule looks at this year and the four before it. It’s a rolling window, not a lifetime ban. Owned a home ten years ago and rented ever since? You likely qualify now.

blocks.text: Contributions are deductible. Money you put in comes off your taxable income, just like an RRSP contribution. You can also save the deduction for a later year, when your income is higher.
Growth is tax-free. While the money sits in the account, growth, interest and dividends aren’t taxed.

Qualifying withdrawals are tax-free too. Take the money out to buy your first qualifying home, and none of it is taxed: not your contributions and not the growth. That’s what makes this account unusual. Most registered accounts give you a break going in or coming out, not both.

What makes a withdrawal qualify. You need a written agreement to buy or build a home in Canada before October 1 of the year after you withdraw, and you must plan to live in it as your main home within a year of buying it. Your bank will ask you to fill out a form (RC725) that confirms these points.
FHSA limits
blocks.detail: Room starts the year you open the account

items.title: Yearly limit
items.text: $8,000 — of new room each calendar year.

items.title: Lifetime limit
Unused room
items.text: Up to $8,000 — carries into the next year, so you can put in as much as $16,000 in one year.

items.title: Account lifespan
items.text: 15 years — or until the end of the year you turn 71, whichever comes first.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: OPEN IT BEFORE YOU’RE READY TO FILL IT

This is the most valuable advice in this lesson, and it costs nothing. FHSA room doesn’t exist until the account does. It doesn’t build up in the background the way TFSA room does. You have to open the account first. Someone who opens an FHSA the year they’re finally ready to buy has missed every year of room they could have built before that. Someone who opens it years earlier, even with a tiny first deposit, starts stacking room right away. If a first home is anywhere on your horizon, opening the account today costs you nothing. Waiting costs you room.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: WHAT HAPPENS IF YOU NEVER BUY

Opening early only makes sense if it’s safe, so here’s what makes it safe. If your plans change and you never buy, the money isn’t lost. Before the account’s deadline, you can move the balance into your RRSP or RRIF tax-free. It doesn’t use up any of your RRSP room, because it moves over on top of the room you already have. You don’t get a second deduction for it, since you already claimed one, but nothing is taxed on the way over. That’s why opening an FHSA as soon as you qualify carries almost no downside.
No 60-day window here. Unlike an RRSP, an FHSA contribution counts only for the calendar year you make it. To use this year’s $8,000 of room, put the money in by December 31.

sections.title: Stacking it with the Home Buyers’ Plan

blocks.text: The FHSA isn’t your only tool. The Home Buyers’ Plan lets you take up to $60,000 out of your RRSP for a first home. Unlike the FHSA, that money must be paid back to your RRSP over 15 years, or the yearly amount you miss is added to your income.
Here’s the part worth knowing: you can use both on the same home. A single buyer can draw up to $100,000 combined. Two first-time buyers purchasing together can draw up to $200,000.
They are different tools, though, and it’s worth keeping them straight.

items.title: “The FHSA and the Home Buyers’ Plan are basically the same thing.”
items.text: They aren’t. FHSA money is never paid back. Once it comes out for a qualifying home, it’s yours. Home Buyers’ Plan money is a loan from your own RRSP, with a real repayment schedule. Using both is smart. Treating them as the same is how people end up owing money back to an RRSP they thought was theirs to keep.

items.title: I haven’t lived in a home I or my spouse owned, this year or in the four years before.
I have an FHSA open, even if I’m not close to buying yet.
I know my current contribution room, not just the annual limit.
If I’m also using the Home Buyers’ Plan, I understand it’s a loan I’ll need to repay, unlike the FHSA.
I know the account must close within 15 years, or by the end of the year I turn 71.

blocks.text: Jamal’s four hundred dollars
paragraphs: Jamal was twenty-six, renting a basement suite in Surrey, and years away from affording a home in the Lower Mainland. Opening a home-buying account felt silly, like planning a wedding before meeting anyone.
Over coffee, a coworker named Lin mentioned that she had opened an FHSA with $100. “The point isn’t being ready to buy,” she said. “The point is having the room waiting for when you are.”

That night Jamal had $400 left over from his paycheque. He could put it toward the new phone he had been eyeing. Or he could try the account Lin had talked about, just to see what the paperwork looked like. He opened the FHSA and put in the $400.

For three years, he added what he could. Some months it was $50, some months nothing. He never treated it as urgent. Each spring, the deduction trimmed his tax bill a little, and his unused room kept rolling forward.

Then came a twist he hadn’t planned for. A promotion arrived two years early, and with it, a small townhouse he could afford. Because he had opened the account early, unused room was waiting for him. He put in $16,000 that year, his $8,000 for the year plus $8,000 carried forward. He deducted it at his new, higher tax rate and took it all out tax-free for his down payment.
Jamal still has the old phone with the cracked screen. He used it to take a photo of his first front door.

blocks.text: The FHSA gives you a tax deduction going in and tax-free withdrawals coming out, a mix no other registered account offers. Room only builds once the account exists, so open one as soon as you qualify, even long before you buy. You can combine it with the Home Buyers’ Plan, but remember: the FHSA never needs paying back, and the Home Buyers’ Plan does.
Open the account now, and your future down payment starts growing tax-free.
blocks.detail: A small first deposit today builds room you can use the year you’re ready to buy.

Answer guidance: if you’re unsure whether you qualify, especially because of a home you owned in the past, check with the CRA rather than guess. If nothing is stopping you from opening an account, that’s your action item: open it this week, whatever your timeline.

items.title: FHSA
items.text: First Home Savings Account. Deductible contributions and tax-free qualifying withdrawals, for first-time home buyers.

items.title: Qualifying withdrawal
items.text: A tax-free withdrawal used to buy a first home that meets the rules.

items.title: Home Buyers’ Plan (HBP)
items.text: A program that lets first-time buyers take money from an RRSP, to be paid back over 15 years.

items.title: First-time home buyer
items.text: Someone who hasn’t lived in a home they or their spouse owned this year or in the four years before.

blocks.text: Educational only, not tax advice. Figures are current for 2026. Confirm them before you contribute.
